meta.title: Olavo de Carvalho — Cronologia
meta.subtitle: Chronology of Olavo de Carvalho (1947–2022): life and works
meta.description: An open, source-referenced chronology of Olavo de Carvalho — journalist, astrologer, self-taught philosopher, teacher of the Curso Online de Filosofia, and the central intellectual reference of the Brazilian New Right.
meta.dataQualityNote: Work-in-progress dataset compiled from public sources (see references). Contested claims — above all his influence on the Bolsonaro government, the cause of his death, and the episodes of his early trajectory — are attributed to their authors, never asserted in this site's voice. Dates not verified against a primary source are flagged. Corrections against primary sources are welcome.

facts.label: Who
facts.value: Olavo Luiz Pimentel de Carvalho — journalist, professional astrologer in the 1980s, self-taught philosopher and polemicist; from 2009 teacher of the Curso Online de Filosofia (COF)

facts.label: Died
facts.value: Night of 24 January 2022, in a hospital in the Richmond, Virginia area (USA), aged 74; announced by the family in the early hours of 25 January. The cause was publicly disputed — see the chronology

facts.label: Residency
facts.value: Brazilian citizen; resident in the United States (Richmond, Virginia area) from 2005 until his death; buried at St. Joseph's Cemetery, Petersburg, Virginia

facts.label: Decorations
facts.value: Medalha do Pacificador (Brazilian Army, 1999); Medalha Mérito Santos Dumont (Brazilian Air Force, 2001); Grã-Cruz of the Ordem de Rio Branco (2019 — contested, see chronology)

facts.label: Family
facts.value: Married to Roxane Andrade de Souza; eight children and eighteen grandchildren at his death

events.title: Born in Campinas, São Paulo
events.text: Born Olavo Luiz Pimentel de Carvalho. Obituaries note he had little formal schooling and described himself as self-taught.

events.title: Brief affiliation with the Brazilian Communist Party (PCB)
events.text: Portuguese Wikipedia dates his PCB affiliation to 1966–1968, in opposition to the military dictatorship; the historian Gilberto Calil likewise records a brief PCB passage in his youth. Exact dates rest on secondary summaries.

events.title: First contributions to Folha de S.Paulo
events.text: Both Wikipedias date his first Folha de S.Paulo piece (in the Folhetim section, on The Magic Flute) to February 1977. Other sources push his journalism back earlier — Gazeta do Povo says he started at 17 at Folha da Manhã; Calil says he began writing for major newspapers in 1967. The sources do not reconcile these, and they may describe different roles.

events.title: Co-founds the Escola Júpiter de Astrologia
events.text: Worked professionally as an astrologer c. 1979–1982, co-founding the school and its Revista de Astrologia Júpiter and collaborating on a university-extension astrology course at PUC-SP; Calil (2021) reports the school had about 140 students by 1980. He later abandoned and disavowed astrology.

events.title: First book: A Imagem do Homem na Astrologia
events.text: Per Portuguese Wikipedia's bibliography. Agência Brasil's obituary instead dates his first book, on astrological symbolism, to 1983 — the sources disagree.

events.title: Enters the Traditionalist / Perennialist milieu
events.text: Per Calil (2021), around 1982 he joined an esoteric 'Tradition' group. Mark Sedgwick, the leading historian of Traditionalism, writes that during the 1980s he was 'first a Traditionalist and then briefly a Maryami and the khalifa of Frithjof Schuon in Brazil'. Approximate dating; all characterizations are these scholars'.

events.title: Involvement with Sufi Islam (the Maryamiyya of Frithjof Schuon)
events.text: Calil (2021) states he converted to Islam in 1984, took the name Sidi Mohammad Ibrahim, and set up a tariqa of his own that dissolved within months. Sedgwick describes him as Schuon's khalifa in Brazil before he 'left Schuon, and reinvented himself as a Catholic philosopher', coining 'post-Traditionalist' for his later fierce criticism of perennialism. All positions attributed; he himself later minimized the episode, and the accounts of it differ.

events.title: Publishes A Nova Era e a Revolução Cultural
events.text: On Gramsci and Fritjof Capra (Instituto de Artes Liberais); obituaries treat it as the book that established him as a conservative polemicist.

events.title: Publishes O Jardim das Aflições
events.text: Subtitled 'de Epicuro à ressurreição de César' (Diadorim); later republished, and the source of the 2017 documentary's title.

events.title: Publishes O Imbecil Coletivo
events.text: His polemic against the Brazilian intelligentsia ('atualidades inculturais brasileiras'); Calil (2021) notes it achieved significant circulation and made him a public figure.

events.title: Publishes Aristóteles em Nova Perspectiva
events.text: His 'theory of the four discourses' reading of Aristotle (Topbooks); year and publisher rest on a single tertiary source.

events.title: Receives the Medalha do Pacificador (Brazilian Army)
events.text: Reported in Agência Brasil's obituary career summary.

events.title: Receives the Medalha Mérito Santos Dumont (Brazilian Air Force)
events.text: Reported in Agência Brasil's obituary career summary.

events.title: Founds the website Mídia Sem Máscara
events.text: A media-criticism site against what it described as leftist bias in the Brazilian press; Calil (2021) treats it as his main ideological platform from 2002 until it went offline around 2017.

events.title: Moves to the United States
events.text: Settled in the Richmond, Virginia area, where he lived until his death; the date is given consistently across obituaries and profiles.

events.title: Begins the online radio program True Outspeak
events.text: Hosted on BlogTalkRadio, 2006–2013, per English Wikipedia (single tertiary source).

events.title: First lecture of the Curso Online de Filosofia (COF)
events.text: The paid weekly online philosophy course he taught until his death — 585 lectures over thirteen years. A student index and English Wikipedia date the first class to 14 March 2009. The community transcription corpus of the course is public (see references); this project cites it by aula and date only.

events.title: Founds the Inter-American Institute for Philosophy, Government, and Social Thought
events.text: Served as its president; English Wikipedia states the institute closed in 2018. Single tertiary source for both dates.

events.title: Written debate with Aleksandr Dugin begins
events.text: The Carvalho–Dugin debate on 'The USA and the New World Order' ran online from 4 March to 31 July 2011, when both published their conclusions; the host site was reportedly accessed by some 200,000 people from over thirty countries.

events.title: The Dugin debate is published as Os EUA e a Nova Ordem Mundial
events.text: Portuguese edition of the debate (VIDE Editorial, trans. Giuliano Moraes); still sold by the official Seminário de Filosofia bookstore.

events.title: Publishes O Mínimo que Você Precisa Saber para Não Ser um Idiota
events.text: 193 press articles from 1997–2013, organized by Felipe Moura Brasil (Record). A best-seller: English Wikipedia cites c. 320,000 copies; Poder360 reports 400,000 combined with O Imbecil Coletivo by 2019 — the figures differ.

events.title: Launches his YouTube channel
events.text: Per Portuguese Wikipedia; the channel passed one million subscribers by his death. Around 2014–2015 he also began public exchanges with Jair Bolsonaro via conservative channels, per English Wikipedia.

events.title: The documentary O Jardim das Aflições premieres
events.text: Josias Teófilo's debut feature about Olavo's life and thought, named after the 1995 book, first screened at Virginia Commonwealth University with Olavo present. An October 2017 screening at UFPE was disrupted — an episode sympathetic outlets described as violent repression (attributed; that account's link is unverified). AdoroCinema catalogs the film as 2015, a discrepancy the sources leave unresolved.

events.title: Mídia Sem Máscara goes offline
events.text: Per Calil (2021), the site operated 2002–2017.

events.title: Bolsonaro's victory-night table displays O Mínimo
events.text: In his election-night livestream, Jair Bolsonaro kept on the table a Bible, the Constitution, a Churchill biography and O Mínimo que Você Precisa Saber para Não Ser um Idiota — widely read by the press as signaling Olavo's status as intellectual reference of the incoming government (that reading is the press's).

events.title: Ernesto Araújo named foreign minister; the press attributes the choice to Olavo
events.text: Fox News (14 November 2018) and other outlets reported Bolsonaro chose the little-known diplomat after Olavo recommended him. Attribution of ministerial picks to Olavo — Araújo at Itamaraty, Ricardo Vélez Rodríguez and later Abraham Weintraub at Education — is a press and academic characterization (Calil 2021; Gazeta do Povo calls him the ministers' 'guru'), which Olavo himself alternately embraced and dismissed.

events.title: The Bolsonaro government takes office with ministers labeled 'olavistas'
events.text: Academics and commentators (Calil 2021; Castro Rocha 2021) describe the Education and Foreign Affairs ministries as staffed on Olavo's recommendation; the press routinely labeled him the government's 'guru' or 'ideologue' — a title he publicly rejected, and which the scholar Mark Sedgwick also considers overstated.

events.title: Awarded the Grã-Cruz of the Ordem de Rio Branco
events.text: Decree published in an extra edition of the Diário Oficial da União on 30 April 2019, giving him the order's highest rank alongside state authorities; Flávio and Eduardo Bolsonaro received the lower Grande Oficial rank in the same decree. A bill in the Chamber of Deputies later sought to annul the concession as contrary to the order's rules — the award remained contested.

events.title: Launch of the online newspaper Brasil Sem Medo
events.text: Poder360's obituary records the 2019 launch, with Olavo as its figurehead.

events.title: Court upholds R$ 2.9 million owed to Caetano Veloso
events.text: Consultor Jurídico reported that his appeal failed against accumulated daily fines plus R$ 65,000 in moral damages, for refusing to delete 2017 social-media posts about the musician Caetano Veloso that the courts had found defamatory. In 2024 CartaCapital reported his heirs were notified of the debt.

events.title: Returns to Brazil for medical treatment
events.text: Poder360's obituary timeline records hospitalizations for pneumonia (February 2021) and respiratory problems (April 2021), travel to Brazil for treatment in July with bladder surgery on 15 July, and readmission for a urinary infection in August.

events.title: Returns to the United States after treatment in Brazil
events.text: Per Poder360's obituary timeline.

events.title: COVID-19 diagnosis announced; course classes suspended
events.text: A message on his Telegram channel dated 15 January 2022 announced the diagnosis and the cancellation of his course classes. Some international outlets date the announcement to 16 January — a minor discrepancy the sources leave open.

events.title: Dies in hospital, aged 74
events.text: The family's statement, posted to his social accounts in the early hours of 25 January, said he died 'na noite de 24 de janeiro' and gave no cause. The cause was publicly disputed: his daughter Heloísa said he 'died of Covid'; his personal physician, Ahmed Youssif El Tassa, stated the death resulted from respiratory failure due to emphysema with heart failure and bacterial pneumonia and was 'not related to COVID'; critical outlets noted the COVID diagnosis announced days earlier and his public minimization of the pandemic. Each position is its author's.

events.title: Bolsonaro decrees one day of official national mourning
events.text: The decree of 25 January 2022 declared official mourning throughout Brazil 'as a sign of grief for the death of Professor Olavo Luiz Pimentel de Carvalho'; Bolsonaro called him 'one of the greatest thinkers in the history of our country'. It was only the second mourning decree of his term.

events.title: Burial at St. Joseph's Cemetery, Petersburg, Virginia
events.text: Per the Find a Grave memorial and English Wikipedia; the exact burial date was not verified from a primary report.

events.title: Heirs notified over the Caetano Veloso judgment debt
events.text: CartaCapital reported that the courts notified his heirs of the R$ 2.9 million owed to Caetano Veloso. The article was verified only via a Wayback snapshot (December 2024); its exact date is unconfirmed.

figures.name: Heloísa de Carvalho
figures.role: Eldest daughter, publicly estranged; stated after his death that her father 'died of Covid'

figures.name: Jair Bolsonaro
figures.role: President of Brazil 2019–2022; decreed national mourning at Olavo's death. The press called Olavo his 'guru' — a label Olavo rejected; Metrópoles reported (attributed) that he 'died resentful' of the Bolsonaro family after their public estrangement from 2020–2021

figures.name: Flávio and Eduardo Bolsonaro
figures.role: Presidential sons and public admirers; Calil dates the family's approach to Olavo to c. 2012–2013. Both received the Ordem de Rio Branco (Grande Oficial) in the same 2019 decree that gave Olavo the Grã-Cruz

figures.name: Ernesto Araújo
figures.role: Foreign minister 2019–2021; his appointment was widely attributed to Olavo's recommendation (Fox News, November 2018)

figures.name: Ricardo Vélez Rodríguez
figures.role: Education minister January–April 2019; appointment attributed by press and academics to Olavo's recommendation

figures.name: Abraham Weintraub
figures.role: Education minister 2019–2020; commonly described as an Olavo-endorsed pick (Gazeta do Povo calls Olavo the 'guru' of ministers Araújo and Weintraub)

figures.name: Aleksandr Dugin
figures.role: Russian ideologue; opponent in the 2011 written debate published as Os EUA e a Nova Ordem Mundial (2012)

figures.name: Frithjof Schuon
figures.role: Perennialist master; per Mark Sedgwick, Olavo was briefly his khalifa in Brazil in the 1980s before breaking with him and becoming a fierce critic of perennialism

figures.name: Josias Teófilo
figures.role: Director of the documentary O Jardim das Aflições (2017), his debut feature

figures.name: Juan Alfredo César Muller
figures.role: Argentine psychologist and astrologer; named as Olavo's astrology teacher (single tertiary source)

figures.name: Stanislavs Ladusans
figures.role: Jesuit philosopher; Olavo studied at his Conpefil center (PUC-Rio) c. 1990–1993 and left without completing a degree after Ladusans's death

figures.name: Ahmed Youssif El Tassa
figures.role: Personal physician; publicly stated the death was from respiratory failure due to emphysema and associated conditions, 'not related to COVID'

figures.name: Felipe Moura Brasil
figures.role: Journalist; selected and organized the 193 articles of O Mínimo (2013)

figures.name: Caetano Veloso
figures.role: Musician; won cumulative fines and damages (R$ 2.9 million upheld in 2020) over 2017 posts the courts found defamatory

figures.name: Mark Sedgwick
figures.role: Historian of Traditionalism (Aarhus University); documents Olavo's Maryamiyya period and coined the 'post-Traditionalist' characterization

figures.name: Gilberto Calil
figures.role: Historian (Unioeste); author of the key critical academic study of Olavo's trajectory (Argumentum, 2021) — critical perspective, labeled as such

figures.name: João Cezar de Castro Rocha
figures.role: Literary scholar (UERJ); analyzes Olavo's rhetoric as central to Bolsonarism in Guerra cultural e retórica do ódio (2021) — critical perspective, labeled as such

organizations.name: Curso Online de Filosofia (COF) / Seminário de Filosofia
organizations.relation: His weekly online philosophy course (585 lectures, 2009–2022) and the platform that continues his courses. The community transcription corpus of the lectures is public and is cited here by aula and date only; the founding date of the earlier in-person Seminário de Filosofia course is not verified

organizations.name: Mídia Sem Máscara
organizations.relation: Founder; his main ideological web platform until it went offline c. 2017 (Calil 2021)

organizations.name: Inter-American Institute for Philosophy, Government, and Social Thought
organizations.relation: Founder and president; closed 2018 per English Wikipedia (single tertiary source for both dates)

organizations.name: Escola Júpiter de Astrologia
organizations.relation: Co-founder, in his professional-astrologer phase; about 140 students by 1980 per Calil

organizations.name: Maryamiyya (tariqa of Frithjof Schuon)
organizations.relation: Member and briefly Schuon's khalifa in Brazil in the 1980s, per Sedgwick; Calil records a 1984 conversion and a short-lived tariqa of his own. All details are these scholars' accounts

organizations.name: Brazilian press (Folha de S.Paulo, O Globo, Jornal da Tarde, Jornal do Brasil, Zero Hora, Época, Bravo!, Primeira Leitura, Diário do Comércio)
organizations.relation: Papers and magazines he wrote for from the 1970s to the 2010s; obituaries list the outlets, but the precise period at each is poorly documented and the Diário do Comércio column's end date is disputed between sources

organizations.name: Gazeta do Povo and Revista Oeste
organizations.relation: Sympathetic outlets he wrote columns for late in life; both identified themselves as publishers of his columns in their obituaries

disambiguation.note: Almost everything about this subject is contested terrain — his title, his influence, his death, and his own retellings of his trajectory. This section records the distinctions the sources themselves make.

items.title: olavodecarvalho.org is no longer his site
items.text: As of August 2026 the live domain returns a page of unrelated e-commerce spam (apparently lapsed and squatted). His actual site must be cited via Internet Archive snapshots (e.g. the 15 December 2021 capture). Do not link the live domain as an official site.

items.title: 'Philosopher' is a claimed and contested title
items.text: He styled himself a philosopher and taught philosophy for decades, but held no degree in the field (he left PUC-Rio's Conpefil without completing studies); mainstream obituaries write 'self-described philosopher', his students insist on the title without qualification. This site records who calls him what.

items.title: Two works named O Jardim das Aflições
items.text: The 1995 book (Diadorim) and the 2017 documentary about him (dir. Josias Teófilo) share the name; AdoroCinema additionally mislabels the film as 2015.

items.title: Not the other Carvalhos
items.text: Not the historian José Murilo de Carvalho (d. 2023), the poet Ronald de Carvalho, or the politician Salatiel Carvalho — search results routinely conflate them.

items.title: 'Guru of Bolsonaro' is an attributed label
items.text: The international press (NYT: 'Bolsonaro's Far-Right Guru') and much of the Brazilian press used the label; Olavo publicly rejected it, and the scholar Mark Sedgwick considers it overstated. It appears on this site only as someone's characterization, never in the site's own voice.

items.title: The COF corpus is cited, not reproduced
items.text: The Curso Online de Filosofia's community transcriptions (585 lectures) are public and of varying review quality, and the lecture header dates carry known defects. This project cites lectures by aula number and date only; the reception index in data/cof-reception.json records which lectures engage which philosopher.

_meta.selection: The ten most engaged philosophers in the COF corpus by the corrected word-boundary measurement (cronologia/archive#44 and its correction comment).
_meta.disciplineNote: Timeline entries assert the philosopher's own public record; the reception layer asserts what Olavo said and when — never what the philosopher 'really' meant (AGENTS.md rule 6). Scholarly date estimates carry approx: true and render with a flag.

philosophers.intro: The ten philosophers most engaged by the Curso Online de Filosofia, by measured presence in the 585-lecture corpus. Each page carries the thinker's own life and works, and the record of which lectures engage him.

philosophers.name: Aristóteles
philosophers.summary: Greek philosopher, disciple of Plato and tutor of Alexander of Macedon, founder of the Lyceum in Athens. His surviving treatises cover logic, physics, biology, metaphysics, ethics, politics, rhetoric and poetics, and shaped much of ancient, medieval and modern philosophy.

timeline.label: Born in Stagira, a small city of Chalcidice in northern Greece.
Moves to Athens and enters Plato's Academy, where he remains for about twenty years as disciple and colleague.
On Plato's death, leaves Athens and settles in Assos, in Asia Minor, with the ruler Hermias.
In Assos and then on the island of Lesbos, pursues research in marine biology; marries Pythias, Hermias's niece.
Summoned by Philip II to the Macedonian court at Pella, becomes tutor of the king's son, the future Alexander the Great (Britannica records 343 or 342 BC).
Returns to Athens and founds his own school, the Lyceum, by the gymnasium dedicated to Apollo Lyceus.

The Lyceum period: composition and organization of most of the surviving corpus — among others the Organon (logic), the Physics, the Metaphysics, the Nicomachean Ethics, the Politics and the Poetics; the internal dating of the treatises is uncertain and debated by specialists.
On Alexander's death and the anti-Macedonian reaction in Athens, withdraws from the city to Chalcis, on the island of Euboea.
Dies in Chalcis, Euboea.

philosophers.name: Descartes
philosophers.summary: French philosopher, mathematician and scientist, often described as the founder of modern philosophy. He created analytic geometry, formulated the first modern version of mind–body dualism, and proposed a method of systematic doubt as the foundation of knowledge.

timeline.label: Born in La Haye, in the Touraine region of France.
Studies at the Jesuit college of La Flèche, following the curriculum of grammar, humanities and scholastic philosophy.
Takes a degree in law at the University of Poitiers, which he will never practice.
Becomes a volunteer soldier at Breda, in the service of Prince Maurice of Nassau; decisive encounter with the scientist Isaac Beeckman.
In the region of Ulm, has the three dreams he interprets as a life mission devoted to the reform of knowledge.
Abandons the Rules for the Direction of the Mind (unfinished) and settles in the Netherlands, where he lives most of his adult life.
Publishes the Discourse on Method, together with the essays Dioptrics, Meteors and Geometry.
Publishes the Meditations on First Philosophy, with the Objections and Replies (2nd edition 1642).
Publishes the Principles of Philosophy, the synthesis of his metaphysics and natural philosophy.
Publishes The Passions of the Soul; accepts Queen Christina of Sweden's invitation and moves to Stockholm.
Dies in Stockholm, after falling ill in the Swedish winter.

philosophers.name: Platão
philosophers.summary: Athenian philosopher, disciple of Socrates and teacher of Aristotle, founder of the Academy. His dialogues, which put into circulation themes such as the theory of Forms, the immortality of the soul and the just city, are among the founding texts of Western philosophy.

timeline.label: Born in Athens to an aristocratic family (the SEP gives '429?'; recent scholarship cited in the SEP's Socrates chronology proposes 424/423 BC).
Death of Socrates, to whose circle Plato belonged; after the execution he leaves Athens and spends a period in Megara, followed by travels the tradition attributes to him (Cyrene, Italy, Egypt).
First journey to Italy and Sicily; in Syracuse he attaches himself to Dion, brother-in-law of the tyrant Dionysius I.
Back in Athens, founds the Academy, the school Britannica places in the 380s BC and describes as a remote ancestor of the modern university.
Dialogues of the so-called early (Socratic) period, on the usual stylometric chronology: Apology, Crito, Euthyphro, Laches, Charmides, Gorgias, Protagoras, among others.
Dialogues of the middle period, including the Phaedo, the Symposium and the Republic (books II–X), in which the theory of Forms is articulated.
Second and third journeys to Syracuse, involving him with Dion in the attempt to influence the young tyrant Dionysius II — episodes narrated in the Seventh Letter, whose authenticity is disputed.
Late dialogues, among them the Theaetetus, Sophist, Statesman, Timaeus, Philebus and the Laws; the corpus transmitted under his name also includes letters and works of disputed authenticity.
Dies in Athens at about eighty; according to Diogenes Laertius he was buried at the Academy.

philosophers.name: Marx
philosophers.summary: German philosopher, economist and revolutionary, author (with Friedrich Engels) of the Communist Manifesto and of Capital. His theory of history, his critique of political economy and the political movement he inspired profoundly marked the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

timeline.label: Born in Trier, in the Rhine province of Prussia.
Enters the University of Bonn (October 1835) and transfers the following year to Berlin, where he studies law and philosophy.
Takes his doctorate in philosophy from the University of Jena.
Becomes editor of the Rheinische Zeitung in Cologne.
Marries Jenny von Westphalen (June) and moves to Paris months later.
Expelled from France, settles in Brussels, followed by Engels; from this period date the manuscripts of The German Ideology (1845–46), published posthumously.
Publishes the Communist Manifesto with Engels, in the year of the European revolutions.
Expelled from Paris once more, settles in London, his home for the rest of his life.
Publishes A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, whose Preface carries the classic formulation of his materialist conception of history.

Foundation of the International Working Men's Association (First International); neither its founder nor its head, Marx becomes its leading intellectual figure, drafting the inaugural address and the provisional statutes.
Publishes volume I of Capital (volumes II and III would appear posthumously, in 1885 and 1894, edited by Engels).
Dies in London.

philosophers.name: Tomás de Aquino
philosophers.place: Roccasecca, near Aquino (Kingdom of Sicily, present-day Italy)
philosophers.summary: Dominican friar, theologian and philosopher, the leading figure of thirteenth-century scholasticism. His synthesis of Aristotelian philosophy and Christian doctrine, set out above all in the Summa theologiae and the Summa contra gentiles, became a central reference of the Catholic tradition.

timeline.label: Born at Roccasecca, a castle of a noble family near Aquino, between Rome and Naples (the SEP gives 'around 1225'; Britannica, '1224/25').
Studies as a child at the Benedictine abbey of Monte Cassino, where his family expected him to make his career.

As an adolescent student at the University of Naples, decides to join the newly founded Order of Preachers (Dominicans) at about twenty; his family, opposed, keeps him detained at Roccasecca for about a year before relenting.
Studies philosophy in Paris as a Dominican friar; in 1248 he is sent to Cologne, under the direction of Albert the Great.
Nominated by Albert, returns to Paris for the advanced degree in theology; composes the commentary on Peter Lombard's Sentences (Scriptum, 1252–56).
Master of theology, holds the Dominican chair at the University of Paris.
Back in Italy, teaches in Dominican houses; composes the Summa contra gentiles (c. 1258–64, per Britannica).
Begins the Summa theologiae, his greatest work, left unfinished at his death (1265/66–73, per Britannica).
Second Paris regency, marked by the controversies over radical Aristotelianism ('Averroism'); writes commentaries on Aristotle's principal works.
Returns to Italy, to Naples, where he spends his last teaching years.
Dies at the Cistercian abbey of Fossanova, in Lazio.

philosophers.name: Kant
philosophers.summary: German philosopher, a central figure of modern philosophy, who spent his whole life in Königsberg. His 'critical philosophy', set out in the three Critiques, proposed that human reason legislates both for the knowledge of nature and for morality.

timeline.label: Born in Königsberg, capital of East Prussia.
Studies at the University of Königsberg (the Albertina); after university, works for some years as a private tutor in the region.
Takes the degree of Magister and becomes Privatdozent (private lecturer) at Königsberg, a position he holds for fifteen years under a heavy teaching load.
Appointed full professor of logic and metaphysics at Königsberg; presents the Inaugural Dissertation, the landmark of his critical turn.
Publishes the Critique of Pure Reason (revised 2nd edition 1787).
Publishes the Prolegomena to Any Future Metaphysics.
Publishes the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, his principal work on the fundamental principle of morality.
Publishes the Critique of Practical Reason.
Publishes the Critique of the Power of Judgment.
Publishes The Metaphysics of Morals (Doctrine of Right and Doctrine of Virtue), after Toward Perpetual Peace (1795).
Dies in Königsberg, the city he never left for long.

philosophers.name: Sócrates
philosophers.summary: Athenian philosopher who wrote nothing, known through the testimonies of Plato, Xenophon and Aristophanes. His practice of interrogating fellow citizens about the virtues, and his condemnation to death for impiety, made him a founding figure of Western philosophical ethics.

timeline.label: Born in Athens, in the deme of Alopece (the SEP, following Nails, gives 469 BC; Britannica records c. 470 BC).
Serves as an infantry soldier (hoplite) in the Potidaea campaign, alongside Alcibiades.
Outbreak of the Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta, the backdrop of his adult life.
Fights at the battle of Delium, an Athenian defeat, under the command of Laches.
Caricatured in Aristophanes' comedy The Clouds, staged at the festival of Dionysus.
Fights at the battle of Amphipolis, another Athenian disaster — his last known campaign.
A member of the presiding committee (prytaneis) by lot, opposes the collective, summary trial of the generals of the battle of Arginusae before the Assembly.
Under the regime of the Thirty, refuses the order to go to Salamis and arrest the democratic general Leon — an episode later recalled in his defense.

Works: he wrote nothing; his thought is known above all through Plato's dialogues, Xenophon's Socratic writings and Aristophanes' satire — the disparity between the portraits constitutes the 'Socratic problem'.
Tried for impiety and for corrupting the young, he is condemned and executed by poison (hemlock) at seventy, in Athens.

philosophers.name: René Guénon
philosophers.summary: French metaphysician and writer, the principal formulator of the twentieth-century 'Traditionalist' or 'Perennialist' current. He wrote on Eastern metaphysics, symbolism, initiation and the critique of the modern world; he embraced Islam and lived his last twenty years in Cairo.

timeline.label: Born in Blois, France; raised in a strict Catholic milieu and educated by Jesuits.
After mathematics studies in Paris (Collège Rollin), abandons preparation for the academic examinations.
Frequents the Parisian occultist and neo-spiritualist milieux — the most obscure period of his biography.
Founds the occultist review La Gnose, which publishes his first writings, already conversant with Vedanta.
Marries a devout Catholic; a new phase of withdrawal from the occultist circles and association with Catholic intellectuals (among them Jacques Maritain).
Publishes his first book, Introduction générale à l'étude des doctrines hindoues, and the critique Le Théosophisme: histoire d'une pseudo-religion; L'Erreur spirite follows in 1923.
Publishes Orient et Occident.
Publishes L'Homme et son devenir selon le Vêdânta, his axial work on Vedanta; L'Ésotérisme de Dante is from the same year.
Publishes La Crise du monde moderne and Le Roi du monde; Catholic criticism of the latter deepens his estrangement from the Church.
Sudden death of his wife.
Travels to Cairo for a three-month stay and remains until his death; openly embraces Islam, is initiated into the Shadhiliyya Sufi order under the name Abdel Wahed Yahya, and remarries.
Publishes Le Règne de la Quantité et les Signes des Temps, considered his masterpiece of the critique of modernity.
Dies in Cairo, Egypt.

philosophers.name: Hegel
philosophers.summary: German philosopher, the leading exponent of post-Kantian German idealism. He elaborated a system spanning logic, philosophy of nature and philosophy of spirit, with lasting influence on philosophy, political theory and the historiography of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

timeline.label: Born in Stuttgart, in the duchy of Württemberg.
Studies at the Protestant seminary of Tübingen (the Stift), where he forms friendships with the poet Hölderlin and the philosopher Schelling.
Moves to Jena, joining Schelling, and publishes his first philosophical work (on the difference between Fichte's and Schelling's systems), along with the dissertation on the orbits of the planets.
Publishes the Phenomenology of Spirit, completed at Jena.
Publishes the Science of Logic, in parts (1812, 1813 and 1816).
Returns to university life as professor at Heidelberg.
Publishes the Encyclopedia of the Philosophical Sciences, the systematic exposition of his thought, later revised in new editions.
Takes the chair of philosophy at the University of Berlin, the most prestigious in the German philosophical world.
Publishes in Berlin the Elements of the Philosophy of Right, his major work of political philosophy.
Dies in Berlin, at the height of his fame.

philosophers.name: Louis Lavelle
philosophers.summary: French philosopher, one of the principal French metaphysicians of the twentieth century and a representative of the 'philosophie de l'esprit' current. Professor at the Sorbonne and the Collège de France, he developed an ontology of participation in being, articulated in the tetralogy La dialectique de l'éternel présent.

timeline.label: Born in Saint-Martin-de-Villeréal, in the Lot-et-Garonne, France.
Teaching career that passes through the University of Strasbourg, before the Sorbonne and the Collège de France.
Publishes La Dialectique du monde sensible.
Professor of philosophy at the Sorbonne.
Publishes La Conscience de soi.
Publishes La Présence totale.
Publishes Le Mal et la souffrance.
Appointed inspector-general of national education and elected to the Collège de France, where he teaches from 1941 to 1951 (a chair opened with the inaugural lecture L'existence et la valeur).
Publishes Du temps et de l'éternité, volume III of the tetralogy La dialectique de l'éternel présent (whose central volume, De l'Acte, is considered his principal work).
Publishes Introduction à l'ontologie; elected to the Académie des sciences morales et politiques.
Dies in the Lot-et-Garonne (Britannica records Saint-Martin-de-Villeréal as the place of death; French sources give neighboring Parranquet).
